bib.title: AutoHarness: improving LLM agents by automatically synthesizing a code harness

legacy_report:
SOURCE: "AutoHarness: improving LLM agents by automatically synthesizing a code harness", Xinghua Lou, Miguel Lázaro-Gredilla, Antoine Dedieu, Carter Wendelken, Wolfgang Lehrach, Kevin P. Murphy (Google DeepMind). arXiv:2603.03329v1 [cs.CL], preprint, dated March 5, 2026 (arXiv stamp says 10 Feb 2026).

COVERAGE: 21 pages, 44,949 chars. Read the abstract, intro, related work, method, experiments, conclusion and appendix text (games table, prompts, signatures, harness code snippet). I read most of the references skimmed. The tail of the D.1 Minesweeper code listing was not read (about the last 15k chars past the printed snippet). Figures 1-7 are images with no extractable numbers. I also read the target note.

CLAIMS (ranked)
- Illegal moves dominate losses for the motivating baseline.
  number: 78%
  setup: Kaggle GameArena chess competition, Gemini-2.5-Flash.
  quote: "in the recent Kaggle GameArena (Kaggle, 2025) chess competition, 78% of losses by Gemini 2.5 Flash were attributed not to strategic blunders, but to simple illegal moves."
  where: p.1-2 (Intro)
- A synthesized harness reached a 100% legal-action rate in all 145 games.
  number: 100% / 1.0 legal action rate, 145 games
  setup: Harness-as-action-verifier, trained with Gemini-2.5-Flash. Measured on novel test rollouts of length 1000 across 10 random seeds per game. TextArena 1P and 2P games, free-form-text games excluded. Valid-move hints removed from observations in some games.
  quote: "The resulting harness prevents all illegal moves in 145 different TextArena games (both 1-player and 2-player)" and "We achieved 100% legal action success rate for all the games as shown in Appendix Table 1."
  where: Abstract; Sec 4.1; Table 1 (p.8-10)
- Training is cheap in iterations.
  number: 14.5 average tree-search iterations; 19/32 games under 10 iterations
  setup: 32 evaluation games. The hardest games listed are GermanWhist, Cryptarithm, Othello and Chess. Table 1 gives Chess-v0 64 learning steps, Othello-v0 62, Breakthrough-v0-small 136 (the maximum), and many games 1.
  quote: "On average, training ends after 14.5 tree search iterations, while 19/32 games end in less than 10 iterations."
  where: Sec 4.1 (p.3)
- The small model plus harness beats the larger model in 2-player games.
  number: 9/16 games, 56.3% vs 38.2%; vs vanilla Flash 12/16 and 64.8%
  setup: 16 2P games, 40 matches per game, split between first and second player. Opponent was Gemini-2.5-Pro. Same optimized prompt for all agents.
  quote: "our approach enables a much smaller Gemini-2.5-Flash to win 9/16 games (overall win rate of 56.3%) against a much larger Gemini-2.5-Pro (overall win rate of 38.2%). When playing against (vanilla) Gemini-2.5-Flash, we win 12/16 games, and the overall win rate rises to 64.8%."
  where: Sec 4.2 (p.4)
- In 1-player games the harness gives a small reward gain.
  number: 0.745 vs 0.707 (Pro) vs 0.673 (Flash); better in 8/16, tied in 5/16
  setup: 16 1P games, 20 runs each, reward metric.
  quote: "On average, we achieve 0.745 reward, in comparison to 0.707 (Gemini-2.5-Pro) and 0.673 (Gemini-2.5-Flash)."
  where: Sec 4.2 (p.4)
- Harness-as-policy (the whole policy as code, no LLM at test time) scored highest.
  number: 0.870 vs GPT-5.2-High 0.844, Gemini-2.5-Pro 0.707, GPT-5.2 0.635. It wins 3/16 games, GPT-5.2-High wins 5/16, and 8/16 tie. Training averaged 89.4 iterations (max 256), heuristic 0.939. Baseline cost was about $640.
  setup: 16 1P games only. Trained with Gemini-2.5-Flash. Heuristic H=0 if illegal, else 0.5+0.5r, with sparse end-of-trajectory reward. 20 runs per game, but only 10 for GPT-5.2 and 5 for GPT-5.2-High, for cost.
  quote: "our approach achieves the highest average reward (0.870), outperforming all other agents including GPT-5.2 (0.635), Gemini-2.5-Pro (0.707), and GPT-5.2-High (0.844)." and "our test time cost is nearly zero, while the GPT-5.2 and GPT-5.2-High experiments cost approximately $640."
  where: Sec 4.3 (p.5)
- Method: the harness is code the LLM writes, and it is a rejection sampler.
  number: none
  setup: Tree search with Thompson sampling (after Tang et al. 2024). The node heuristic is average legal-move accuracy, with heuristic weight 1.0. The LLM acts as the mutation operator. Each iteration uses 10 parallel environments, rollouts of up to 1000 steps, and at most 5 failed steps fed to a Critic, then a Refiner. Two functions are learned, `propose_action()` and `is_legal_action()`. If `is_legal_action` returns True but the action is invalid, both are refined. If it returns False and the action is invalid, only `propose_action` is refined.
  quote: "In its simplest incarnation, the harness can be seen as a control loop that calls the LLM and rejects unacceptable answers. The definition of what is acceptable is itself learned. This essentially results in a rejection sampler for LLMs in which the conditioning is learned based on the task."
  where: Sec 1, 3 (p.1-3)
- Three harness variants are defined.
  number: none
  setup: action-filter, action-verifier and policy. Only the verifier and policy are evaluated.
  quote: "harness-as-action-filter calls propose_action() to generate a set of legal moves, and leverages the LLM to rank them"; "harness-as-action-verifier first calls the LLM to generate an action, verifies it by is_legal_action(), and, if invalid, repeats the process with a new prompt that includes an 'illegal action' warning message"
  where: Sec 3 (p.3)
- Hand-written harnesses and fine-tuning are named as the alternatives.
  number: none
  quote: "Hand-designed harnesses are brittle and labor-intensive, requiring additional work for every new game."
  where: p.1

LIMITS
- One harness per environment, learned from environment feedback. The authors want a reusable library and distillation back into the base model (Sec 5).
- Only games were tested, with a simulator that reports legality. No real tool-use, shell or security setting. Nothing is said about sandboxing, permissions or adversarial agents.
- Harness-as-policy is 1P only. 2P would need an opponent model or a code world model (footnote 3).
- Evaluation covers 32 of 145 games "for efficiency". Valid-move hints were removed only in some games ("we modified some games").
- "Legal action rate" is the fraction of legal actions in rollouts. It is not proof of coverage for unseen states.
- No variance, confidence intervals or significance tests reported. Only Gemini-2.5 and GPT-5.2 were tested, and the GPT-5.2 baselines had fewer repeats.
- The paper never measures a reward gain for the verifier harness in terms of cost. The cost claim is only for the policy variant.

BUILDS ON: Tang et al. 2024 (code repair as an exploration-exploitation trade-off, Thompson sampling); Liang et al. 2023 (Code as Policies); Voyager (Wang et al. 2023); Eureka (Ma et al. 2024); Reflexion (Shinn et al. 2023); AlphaCode (Li et al. 2022); AlphaEvolve (Novikov et al. 2025); Code World Models (Lehrach et al. 2025); TextArena (Guertler et al. 2025); action applicability in planning (Kokel et al. 2025); Tree of Thoughts (Yao et al. 2023).

Refiner prompt (B.2) includes: "Make sure to only produce code that is safe to execute." and "Do not use any the try-except blocks."

FIGURES: Fig 1 (p.3) code-as-harness learning loop: rollout, critic, refiner, evaluator. Fig 2 (p.4) legal-move fraction against refinement count for 6 games. Fig 3 (p.4) 2P win/draw/loss vs Pro. Fig 4 (p.5) 1P reward vs Pro. Fig 5 (p.5) 1P average reward across six agents. Fig 6-7 (p.11) per-game reward and legal rate. Run `scripts/papers/figures.py captions` for exact captions.

FIT TO NOTE 04-execution-boundaries.md (facts for the caller, no verdict)
- The paper is about rule-legality in games, not security boundaries. It supports "enforce in code, not prose" only by analogy: an `is_legal_action` verifier outside the model rejects invalid output and retries with a warning.
- The note does not currently cite it. The relevant point is that the code check is generated and refined from environment feedback rather than hand-written.
- The note's "Fail closed" / hook material (Li, Lin et al.) is independent. The paper makes no claim about injection, sandboxes or permissions, so it should not be cited for those.

PROBLEMS: No embedded instructions found. Extraction was clean text. Figures contain no extractable data, so per-game values for Figs 3-7 are not read. The arXiv header says 10 Feb 2026 while the cover date is March 5, 2026.
